# Introduction & Question

Youth mental health has become an increasingly important public health concern in Canada and around the world. Research has documented declines in self-reported mental health among adolescents in recent years, potentially exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic and its related disruptions. These changes may not have been experienced equally across groups, as young people's mental health and vulnerabilities can vary by developmental stage and social and structural factors like race, class, and, for the purposes of this project, gender. Investigating variation across these groups may help us understand who is most vulnerable and where supports and interventions may be most needed.

This analysis uses Statistics Canada's Canadian Health Survey on Children and Youth to examine changes in the percentage of Canadian youth reporting excellent or very good mental health between 2019 and 2023. Specifically, I compare boys+ and girls+ in two age groups, 12–14 and 15–17 in 2019 (approximately 16-18 and 19-21, respectively, in 2023).

**Research question:** How did the percentage of Canadian youth reporting excellent or very good mental health change between 2019 and 2023, and how did these changes vary by age and gender?

# Setup, Cleaning, and Testing

## Setup

First things first: reading in my data! My data comes from [here](https://open.canada.ca/data/en/dataset/ef44c64a-6f75-443b-a691-28d232c14587/resource/0dd7da70-2c13-4efb-ba83-a65978001f00).

```{r}
# loading in the necessary packages
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
```

```{r}
# import the Statscan dataset
my_data <- read.csv("../data/data_story_data.csv")

# inspect the column names
names(my_data)
```

## Initial Inspection

Before making any changes, I want to inspect the dataset and check the variables and categories it contains.

```{r}
# examine the number of rows and columns
dim(my_data)
# inspect variable types and dataset structure
str(my_data)

# examine the unique categories in each of the key variables
unique(my_data$GEO)
unique(my_data$Indicators)
unique(my_data$`Age group in 2019`)
unique(my_data$`Gender in 2019`)
unique(my_data$Status)
unique(my_data$Characteristics)

# check for any missing values across all columns
colSums(is.na(my_data))
```

Let's take a look.

```{r}
# preview the data
head(my_data)

tail(my_data)
```

```{r}
# get an overview of the variables and their types
glimpse(my_data)
```

I see that there are NAs in the "Symbol" and "Terminated" columns. These are metadata fields that do not affect the mental health reporting numbers.

## Selecting and Cleaning Relevant Data

First, I am selecting just my indicator of interest, which is perceived mental health rated as excellent or very good. I am also limiting the data to just Canada rather than including provincial estimates.

```{r}
# remove provincial level estimates and other health indicators 
my_data <- my_data |>
  filter(
    GEO == "Canada",
    Indicators == "Perceived mental health, excellent or very good"
  )

head(my_data)
```

Renaming the column names next, for clarity:

```{r}
# rename relevant columns
names(my_data)[names(my_data) == "Age.group.in.2019"] <- "Age_group"
names(my_data)[names(my_data) == "Gender.in.2019"] <- "Gender"
names(my_data)[names(my_data) == "Indicators"] <- "Indicator"
names(my_data)[names(my_data) == "Characteristics"] <- "MetricType"
names(my_data)[names(my_data) == "VALUE"] <- "Value"

names(my_data)
```

Now I want to remove the "total" categories for both age and gender, since I am interested in comparing the two age groups and two gender categories separately:

```{r}
# remove age group = total and gender = total groups
my_data <- my_data |>
  filter(
    Age_group != "Total, 12 to 17 years",
    Gender != "Total, Gender+"
  )

head(my_data)
```

I am also filtering out all metrics other than "number of persons," as I want to calculate percentages myself rather than relying on the ones provided.

```{r}
# retain only observations reporting the number of persons
my_data <- my_data |>
  filter(MetricType == "Number of persons")

head(my_data)
```

## Checking Variable Types and Values

Now I want to check that the value column is numeric, since I will be using it to calculate percentages and changes.

```{r}
# inspect the cleaned dataset structure and confirm that values are numeric
str(my_data)
is.numeric(my_data$Value)

# check the remaining age, gender, and reporting status categories to make sure the intended groups were retained 
unique(my_data$Age_group)
unique(my_data$Gender)
unique(my_data$Status)
```

Looks good!

## Combining Categories

Since I am interested in comparing 2019 and 2023, I need to combine some of the reporting categories. "Reported indicator in 2019 only" and "Reported indicator in 2019 and 2023" will be combined to calculate the percentage reporting excellent or very good mental health in 2019. Similarly, "Reported indicator in 2023 only" and "Reported indicator in 2019 and 2023" will be combined to calculate the percentage for 2023.

```{r}
# standardize the whitespace in the original status levels to prevent inconsistencies from interfering with recoding
my_data$Status <- stringr::str_squish(my_data$Status)

# simplify the original reporting status labels
my_data <- my_data |>
  mutate(
    Status = case_when(
      Status == "Reported indicator in 2019 only" ~ "2019_only",
      Status == "Reported indicator in 2023 only" ~ "2023_only",
      Status == "Reported indicator in 2019 and 2023" ~ "both",
      Status == "Did not report indicator in 2019 and 2023" ~ "neither"
    )
  )

# check the resulting status categories
unique(my_data$Status)
```

Now, reshaping the data so each status becomes its own column:

```{r}
# reshape the data from long to wide format, each status category becomes its own column
reshaped_data <- my_data |>
  select(Age_group, Gender, Status, Value) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = Status,
    values_from = Value
  )

reshaped_data
```

## Calculating Change

First let's create total categories for 2019 and 2023.

```{r}
# combine categories so that "both" is included in 2019 and 2023
# calculate the difference between counts for 2023 and 2019
reshaped_data <- reshaped_data |>
  mutate(
    number_2019 = `2019_only` + both,
    number_2023 = `2023_only` + both,
    change = number_2023 - number_2019
  )

reshaped_data
```

Now I can look at the distribution of change by age and gender. I will calculate percents and add that as a column.

```{r}
# calculate the total population represented by the four status categories 
# use this total as the denominator to calculate the percentage for each year
reshaped_data <- reshaped_data |>
  mutate(
    total_pop = `2019_only` + `2023_only` + both + neither,
    pct_2019 = (number_2019 / total_pop) * 100,
    pct_2023 = (number_2023 / total_pop) * 100,
    pct_point_change = pct_2023 - pct_2019
  )

reshaped_data
```

## Testing

First, I will check that the four reporting categories account for the entire population represented in each age/gender group by confirming that their percentages sum to approximately 100%.

```{r}
# calculate the percentage represented by each category and make sure they sum to approx. 100%
status_totals <- reshaped_data |>
  mutate(
    pct_2019_only = `2019_only` / total_pop * 100,
    pct_2023_only = `2023_only` / total_pop * 100,
    pct_both = both / total_pop * 100,
    pct_neither = neither / total_pop * 100,
    total_percentage = pct_2019_only + pct_2023_only +
      pct_both + pct_neither
  )

status_totals

# return TRUE if the four categories account for approximately 100% of each group's population
all(abs(status_totals$total_percentage - 100) < 0.01)
```

I will also now check for any missing or invalid values. This should return TRUE for all ten lines.

```{r}
# check that the population totals are present and positive
all(!is.na(reshaped_data$total_pop))
all(reshaped_data$total_pop > 0)

# confirm that none of the four status counts are missing
all(!is.na(reshaped_data$`2019_only`))
all(!is.na(reshaped_data$`2023_only`))
all(!is.na(reshaped_data$both))
all(!is.na(reshaped_data$neither))

# confirm that none of the status counts are negative 
all(reshaped_data$`2019_only` >= 0)
all(reshaped_data$`2023_only` >= 0)
all(reshaped_data$both >= 0)
all(reshaped_data$neither >= 0)
```

Finally, I will check to make sure the right number of age/gender groups are present:

```{r}
# confirm that the filtering and reshaping produced the four expected categories 
nrow(reshaped_data) == 4

n_distinct(reshaped_data$Age_group, reshaped_data$Gender) == 4
```

Good to go!

# Exploratory Analysis

First, I will reshape my data into a format that is more suitable for plotting:

```{r}
# reshape the data into long format so that 2019 and 2023 percentages can be separate points on the same graph
plot_data <- reshaped_data |>
  select(Age_group, Gender, pct_2019, pct_2023) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(pct_2019, pct_2023),
    names_to = "Year",
    values_to = "Percentage"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Year = recode(
      Year,
      pct_2019 = "2019",
      pct_2023 = "2023"
    )
  )

plot_data
```

Now let's make a graph comparing 2019 and 2023!

```{r}
plot_data <- plot_data |>
  mutate(
    Group = case_when(
      Age_group == "12 to 14 years" & Gender == "Boys+" ~ "Boys, 12–14",
      Age_group == "15 to 17 years" & Gender == "Boys+" ~ "Boys, 15–17",
      Age_group == "12 to 14 years" & Gender == "Girls+" ~ "Girls, 12–14",
      Age_group == "15 to 17 years" & Gender == "Girls+" ~ "Girls, 15–17"
    )
  )

ggplot(plot_data, aes(
  x = Year,
  y = Percentage,
  color = Group,
  group = Group
)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  ylim(20,90) + 
  labs(
    title = "Changes in Excellent or Very Good Mental Health, 2019–2023",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Percentage",
    color = "Age and Gender"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

And as a percentage point change:

```{r}
ggplot(reshaped_data, aes(x = Gender, y = pct_point_change, fill = Gender)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~ Age_group) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  ylim(-35,0) +
  labs(
    title = "Change in Excellent or Very Good Mental Health, 2019–2023",
    x = "Gender",
    y = "Change (percentage points)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  guides(fill = "none")
```

These two graphs clearly show that girls aged 12-14 in 2019 experienced the biggest decline in percentage reporting excellent/very good mental health from 2019-2023.

Lastly, I'm curious to see the share of each gender/age group that reported excellent/very good mental health in 2019 only, 2023 only, both, and neither.

```{r}
# pivoting the data longer so that reporting status goes from four discrete columns to one variable with four choices
status_data <- reshaped_data |>
  select(Age_group, Gender, `2019_only`, `2023_only`, both, neither, total_pop) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(`2019_only`, `2023_only`, both, neither),
    names_to = "Status",
    values_to = "Count"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Percentage = (Count / total_pop) * 100,
    Status = recode(
      Status,
      "2019_only" = "2019 only",
      "2023_only" = "2023 only",
      "both" = "Both years",
      "neither" = "Neither year"
    )
  )
```

```{r}
ggplot(status_data, aes(
  x = Gender,
  y = Percentage,
  fill = Status
)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~ Age_group) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Reporting Across 2019 and 2023",
    x = "Gender",
    y = "Percentage of group",
    fill = "Reporting status"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

I can see that girls aged 15-17 were the most likely to not report excellent/very good mental health in either year, and boys 12-14 were most likely to report it in both years. Girls 12-14 were most likely to report it in 2019 only, consistent with the other graphs showing this group had the biggest decline.

# Reflections and Surprises

Looking at these graphs, I was surprised that the group with the lowest overall reporting of excellent/very good mental health was not the same as the group that had the largest decline from 2019 to 2023. Girls aged 15-17 were most likely to fall into the "neither year" category whereas girls 12-14 experienced the largest percentage point decline. This is interesting and adds another dimension of difference between groups to my analysis (overall reporting levels vs. change over time).

In terms of the data itself, I was not necessarily surprised by anything in the structure, but I had to think carefully about how to create the total categories for each year. The existing categories imposed by Statscan (2019 only, 2023 only, both, neither) made some extra steps necessary for me to create the categories I wanted for my analysis.
